projects.title: Smart Pill Dispenser
projects.name: Autonomous Pill Dispenser
projects.description: A fully self-contained dispenser that releases medication at a scheduled time and confirms removal before silencing — designed, built, and tested independently, including a custom 3D-printed enclosure.
projects.highlight: Merged multiple firmware subsystems (RTC scheduling, alarm state, photoresistor detection) onto one Arduino Nano; resolved a flag-reset bug in the alarm window logic during integration.
writeup: The goal was a dispenser that needed no daily attention beyond loading pills and setting a schedule: it wakes up, checks the time against a stored alarm, rotates a chamber to release a dose, then confirms the pill was actually removed before going quiet again.

Timekeeping runs on a DS3231 real-time clock rather than the Arduino's internal timer, since internal clocks drift over days — the DS3231's oscillator bit (EOSC) was explicitly configured to keep it powered and accurate even between resets.

The trickiest part wasn't any single component — it was merging the stepper control, alarm-state logic, potentiometer-based schedule setting, and OLED display code into one coherent state machine without variable name collisions or state conflicts. A flag-reset bug in the alarm window logic (where the 'has this dose been given' flag wasn't clearing correctly between cycles) took a full debugging session to isolate and fix.

The enclosure was fully modeled in Onshape and printed in PETG on a Bambu Lab P1S, with the lid, lid-attachment interface, and internal Arduino mount all designed as separate testable components before final assembly.

projects.title: Solar Oven + Custom PCB
projects.name: Passive Solar Oven with Digital Readout
projects.description: A passive solar oven using layered insulation and a clear top to concentrate heat, with a live temperature readout built around a custom PCB — my first designed-from-scratch board.
projects.highlight: Laid out the schematic and board in KiCad, hand-soldered through-hole components, and verified it against the working breadboard prototype.
writeup: The oven itself is a passive design — layered insulating materials with a clear top to trap and concentrate solar heat, no electronics required to actually cook. The electronics layer on top is purely for monitoring: a live digital readout of internal temperature.

Temperature sensing uses a DS18B20 waterproof thermal probe, chosen for its digital output (no analog calibration drift) and tolerance for the oven's internal heat. The reading drives a 4-digit 7-segment display through an SN74HC595N shift register, which cuts the number of Arduino pins needed from what direct-driving four digits would require.

After validating the circuit on a breadboard, I moved it into KiCad to design a proper schematic and PCB layout — my first board designed completely from scratch rather than assembled point-to-point. The board was fabricated externally and hand-soldered using through-hole components, then re-tested against the original breadboard version to confirm nothing was lost in translation.

projects.title: Pole-Climbing Robot
projects.name: Autonomous Pole-Climbing Robot
projects.description: Led my school's build for UBC's Physics Olympics prebuild event: a motorized robot designed to climb a pipe carrying a 170g payload, with custom-printed gearing to boost torque.
projects.highlight: A loose alligator-clip connection disconnected mid-run, causing disqualification. Now I design for strain relief and connector security, not just bench-test continuity.
writeup: UBC's Physics Olympics prebuild event set a clear physical challenge: build a robot that climbs a vertical pipe under its own power while carrying a fixed payload (a 170g phone) as fast and reliably as possible. I led my school's team through the design and build.

The drivetrain used a DC motor controlled through an L293D H-Bridge IC, run from an Arduino Uno — the H-Bridge allowed direct control over motor direction and speed rather than relying on a simpler one-direction driver. Torque was the main constraint: climbing against gravity with a real payload needed more mechanical advantage than the motor alone provided, so I designed and 3D-printed a custom gear adapter to increase torque at the cost of speed.

On competition day, the robot worked in every practice run — but an alligator-clip connection between the motor and battery worked loose during the actual run, cutting power mid-climb and disqualifying the team. It was a genuinely useful lesson: a connection that's fine on a bench, sitting still, isn't automatically fine under real vibration and handling. Strain relief and connector security are now a standard part of how I think about any build meant to actually move.

projects.title: Solar Power Bank
projects.name: Solar Power Bank
projects.description: Power electronics project which uses an XL6009 buck-boost module to convert the 5.5V 6W output of a solar panel to a stable 5V, which is then routed to a power bank breakout board, charging 2 18650 batteries in parralel, which can be discharged to a phone later.
projects.highlight: This project went through the most iterations out of any of my projects. I learned a lot about the engineering design cycle and power electronics through improving my ideas here.
writeup: The plan started out simple. I had a spare 12V solar panel lying around from a failed solar-boat project a few years ago, and a solar-powered phone charger seemed like a great idea for a project that would end up with something I could actually USE, learning about power electronics along the way.

However, it wasn't that simple. Initially, I attempted to use a 12V 2W solar panel to charge a phone directly, however, this had a lot of issues. Firstly, modern iPhones are rather picky about their charging inputs - I needed to solder two CC resistors into my USB breakout board before the iphone would accept a charge, and if the output wasn't stable enough, the iphone would refuse to charge. Secondly, the solar panel I was using just wasn't strong enough. 12V was impressive, and it measued an open circuit voltage of over 17V in ideal sunlight, but the short circuit current (Isc) I measured was only 52mA, giving the panel a power output of 0.884W, less than half of the advertised 2W output, which was already very low.

I attempted to make it work anyways, charging a power bank I bought. After plugging the solar panel into the power bank's input, the charging light lit up, but the wattage of the panel just wasn't sufficient, causing the input voltage to sag all the way from 17V to 2.2V; the bank would never even go up a single percent.

I swapped out the old solar panel for a higher quality 6W panel from waveshare, and it charged my storebought power bank, leading me to improve my project further by creating my own power bank using a module I purchased and two Li 18650 batteries
